title: Learning to Recall with Transformers Beyond Orthogonal Embeddings
abstract:
Modern large language models (LLMs) excel at tasks that require storing and retrieving knowledge, such as factual recall and question answering. Transformers are central to this capability, thanks to their ability to encode information during training and retrieve it at inference. Existing theoretical analyses typically study transformers under idealized assumptions such as infinite data or orthogonal embeddings. In realistic settings, however, models are trained on finite datasets with non-orthogonal (random) embeddings. 
We address this gap by analyzing a single-layer transformer with random embeddings trained with (empirical) gradient descent on a simple token-retrieval task, where the model must identify an informative token within a length-$L$ sequence and learn a one-to-one mapping from tokens to labels. Our analysis tracks the "early phase" of gradient descent and yields explicit formulas for the model’s storage capacity—revealing a multiplicative dependence between sample size $N$, embedding dimension $d$, and sequence length $L$. We complement this with a lower bound for the statistical problem, showing that this multiplicative scaling is inherent under non-orthogonal embeddings.
problem: Existing theoretical analyses of transformers assume idealized settings like infinite data or orthogonal embeddings, but realistic settings use finite data with non-orthogonal random embeddings.
approach: They analyze a single-layer transformer with random embeddings trained on a token-retrieval task, tracking early-phase gradient descent to derive explicit storage capacity formulas revealing multiplicative dependence between sample size, embedding dimension, and sequence length.
contribution: They provide explicit formulas for model storage capacity and lower bounds demonstrating that multiplicative scaling is inherent under non-orthogonal embeddings.
